h1:
Wat Burapha Phiram
Luang Pho Yai, Thailand's Tallest Standing Buddha
intro: Drive into Roi Et town and you'll spot a huge standing Buddha rising above the rooftops from a long way off. That's Luang Pho Yai at Wat Burapha Phiram, the tallest standing Buddha in Thailand and a temple local families have come to for generations to pay respects and make a wish.

blocks.html: Wat Burapha Phiram really is right in the middle of Roi Et town — just a few minutes' walk from Bueng Phlan Chai. The thing everyone comes for is Luang Pho Yai, full name Phra Phuttha Rattana Mongkhon Maha Muni, the tallest standing Buddha in Thailand at 59.20 metres, or 67.85 metres if you count the base. It stands tall enough to see from all over town, and if you only have time for one stop in Roi Et, most locals will point you here.

blocks.text: Luang Pho Yai, Thailand's tallest standing Buddha

blocks.html: The image is built of reinforced concrete, started back in 1973. It's a standing Buddha in the gesture of granting blessings (pang prathan phon), facing east. At 59.20 metres it's about as tall as a several-dozen-storey building, and standing at the base looking straight up, you really feel the scale. The height is also tied to the province's name — it's meant to evoke 101 (Roi Et means "one hundred and one") in local belief.

Beneath the base of the image there's a hall, with stairs leading up so you can pay respects and make merit inside. It stays cool and shaded, and people come to apply gold leaf, offer flowers, and make a wish — especially about work and travel, since this is the blessing-granting pose.

blocks.title: Photo tip
blocks.html: To get the whole Buddha in frame, step back and shoot from the front courtyard. In the morning the sun lights up the front of the image nicely, while late in the day near closing (around 4 pm) the sky turns soft and there are fewer people around.

blocks.text: Temple history: why it's tied to the town

blocks.html: Wat Burapha Phiram is a third-class royal temple under the Maha Nikaya order, founded back in 1913. It was originally called Wat Hua Ro because it used to be a rest stop for travelling merchants. Later it became Wat Burapha (the eastern temple), after its location on the east side of town, and finally Wat Burapha Phiram as it's known today.

The eastern side of the temple borders the old city moat of Roi Et, so this isn't just a pretty temple — it's been tied to the town's history from the start. Inside you'll also find mural paintings telling the story of the Buddha's life and Isan traditions, and the temple is home to a Dhamma propagation centre and a Pali studies school.

blocks.text: Before you go: hours, entry, and getting there

items: Opening hours — Open daily, roughly 8:30 am–4:30 pm (free entry, no admission fee)
Address — 559 Phadung Phanit Road, Nai Mueang sub-district, Mueang Roi Et district, within the town municipality
Getting there — Right in the town centre; about a 5–10 minute walk from Bueng Phlan Chai, or an easy tuk-tuk / local taxi ride
Parking — There's a fair-sized lot inside the temple; quiet on weekdays, busier on weekends and Buddhist holy days
Dress code — Dress modestly, shoulders and knees covered, since it's a religious site

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: Wat Burapha Phiram doesn't take long to see — about 30–45 minutes and you've covered it. The main draw is Luang Pho Yai; this isn't a sprawling temple with multiple zones to wander all day. So it pairs better with other nearby spots in town than as a stop on its own.

blocks.text: Where to go next, all in one day

blocks.html: The nice thing about Wat Burapha Phiram is that it's central — a few minutes on foot or by car gets you to the next sight, so you can easily put together a half-day around Roi Et town.

items.name: Bueng Phlan Chai
items.blurb: A public park built around an island in the middle of a lake — stroll, cycle, feed the fish. It's right next to the temple, practically across the road.

items.name: Ho Wot 101 Tower
items.blurb: An observation tower shaped like a wot (Isan reed pipe). Head up for 360-degree views of Roi Et, looking down on Luang Pho Yai and Bueng Phlan Chai.

items.name: Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon
items.blurb: A massive white-and-gold pagoda in Nong Phok district, a bit of a drive out of town — great for a temple-and-merit road trip.

faq.q: What time does Wat Burapha Phiram open, and is there an entry fee?
faq.a: It's open daily, roughly 8:30 am–4:30 pm, and entry is free with no admission fee. If you'd like to make merit, there are donation boxes and a spot inside the temple to offer flowers, incense, and gold leaf.

faq.q: How tall is Luang Pho Yai at Wat Burapha Phiram?
faq.a: Phra Phuttha Rattana Mongkhon Maha Muni (Luang Pho Yai) is 59.20 metres tall, or 67.85 metres including the base. It's the tallest standing Buddha in the blessing-granting pose in Thailand, built in 1973.

faq.q: Where in Roi Et is Wat Burapha Phiram, and is it hard to reach?
faq.a: It's right in central Roi Et on Phadung Phanit Road, Nai Mueang sub-district, very close to Bueng Phlan Chai — you can walk between the two. If you're coming from out of town, just drive in and park inside the temple.

faq.q: How long should I spend at the temple?
faq.a: About 30–45 minutes covers it. The main things to do are paying respects to Luang Pho Yai and going up to make merit beneath the base. It's worth pairing with Bueng Phlan Chai and the Ho Wot 101 Tower nearby to make the trip worthwhile.

faq.q: What should I wear to Wat Burapha Phiram?
faq.a: Dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered, since it's a royal temple and a religious site. A T-shirt with long trousers or a knee-length skirt is tidy enough.
